canonical_statement: The study was designed to determine how renal impairment affects cefazolin persistence in serum and the ability to achieve urinary concentrations, with additional comparisons to cephalothin and observations on protein binding and hemodialysis removal.
Six healthy volunteers were enrolled as the normal-renal-function group.

population.label: Healthy volunteers with normal renal function

canonical_statement: Eleven patients with varying degrees of renal impairment were enrolled.
All six healthy volunteers and four uremic patients received single 500 mg intramuscular injections of cefazolin and cephalothin at least one week apart.

population.label: Six healthy volunteers and four uremic patients

exposures.details: single dose; at least one week apart from cefazolin in comparative subjects

canonical_statement: The remaining seven patients with impaired renal function received a single intramuscular cefazolin regimen without the cephalothin comparison.
For four days, the six normal subjects received cefazolin 500 mg intramuscularly every 8 hours.
Two uremic patients received cefazolin 500 mg as a loading dose followed by 250 mg approximately once each individual drug half-life: every 12 hours in one patient and every 24 hours in the other.

exposures.frequency: every 12 hours in one patient and every 24 hours in the other

canonical_statement: After antibiotic administration, venous blood was sampled through 12 hours in all subjects and through 48 hours in those with significant renal impairment; urine was collected in sequential intervals through 48 hours.
Cefazolin and cephalothin in serum and urine were measured by a cup-plate bioassay using Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 6538P.
Serum protein binding was measured by equilibrium dialysis, and measured binding percentages were used to estimate free-drug concentrations.

Creatinine clearance was measured on successive days; serum concentration decline was fit by least-squares regression for half-life and elimination rate, and apparent volume of distribution was estimated with a one-compartment open model using nonlinear regression.
In normal volunteers given equivalent 500 mg intramuscular doses, peak total cefazolin serum concentrations were approximately four- to sixfold those of cephalothin.

exposures.details: single dose; at least one week apart from cefazolin in comparative subjects

canonical_statement: In normal volunteers given equivalent 500 mg intramuscular doses, free cefazolin concentrations in serum were about threefold those of cephalothin.

canonical_statement: In severely uremic patients, adequate free cefazolin concentrations were maintained for at least 48 hours after a single intramuscular dose.

concept.text: Persistence of free cefazolin concentration in serum

canonical_statement: After a single intramuscular dose in normal subjects, mean serum half-life was 1.91 ± 0.23 hours for cefazolin and 0.58 ± 0.11 hours for cephalothin.

canonical_statement: Cefazolin serum half-life lengthened as renal function declined, with a sharp increase when creatinine clearance fell below 20 mL/min; cephalothin half-life increased more modestly.

canonical_statement: Among patients with renal impairment, cefazolin protein binding ranged from 61.6% to 84.7%.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: lower bound of reported cefazolin protein-binding range

canonical_statement: In vitro cefazolin binding in subjects with normal renal function was not significantly reduced until serum albumin was below 3.0 g/100 mL, whereas uremic patients showed marked binding variability with no apparent correlation to albumin despite most having albumin above 3.0 g/100 mL.

The renal-patient group with the lowest mean cefazolin protein binding (63.4% ± 1.5%) had an apparent volume of distribution of 23.0% ± 4.3% of body weight versus 12.2% ± 3.4% in normal subjects; the volume difference was reported as P<0.01.
Renal group 2 (creatinine clearances 3, 4, 12, and 15 mL/min) had a mean peak cefazolin serum concentration of 65.5 ± 11.7 µg/mL versus 42.9 ± 7.3 µg/mL in normal subjects, reported as P<0.01.
In normal volunteers, urinary recovery of cefazolin was virtually complete within 12 hours, with an average recovery of 74.2% of the dose.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: mean percent of dose recovered in urine

canonical_statement: Eight-hour urinary recovery of cefazolin was related to creatinine clearance by y = 2.33x^0.73 with r = 0.926.
Patients with creatinine clearance ≤15 mL/min had peak urinary cefazolin concentrations ranging from 175 to 400 µg/mL despite reduced urinary excretion.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: lower bound of reported peak urinary concentration range

canonical_statement: During four days of cefazolin 500 mg intramuscularly every 8 hours in normal subjects, mean peak serum concentration was 52.8 µg/mL and was approximately unchanged across the four treatment days.
During the normal-subject multiple-dose study, average maximal and minimal urinary cefazolin concentrations were 2,200 and 400 µg/mL, respectively.

In two uremic patients given a 500 mg loading dose followed by 250 mg at intervals approximately equal to individual cefazolin half-life, serum concentrations ranged from 36.9 to 78.0 µg/mL over four days without significant accumulation.

canonical_statement: Cefazolin was reported to be well tolerated when administered intramuscularly, but the article did not provide a quantitative adverse-event table.

The authors considered cefazolin a promising cephalosporin because it produced higher and more prolonged free-drug concentrations while having antimicrobial activity similar to cephalothin; they stated that its ultimate role would depend on toxicity and cost.
The authors stated that the optimal cefazolin dose and dosage interval in patients with normal renal function still required determination in clinical trials.

Based on extrapolation from free-drug levels relative to cephalothin, the authors proposed that either half the dose or twice the customary cephalothin dosing interval should be at least equivalent in patients with normal renal function.

For relatively safe penicillins and cephalosporins in renal impairment, the authors preferred a loading dose followed by one-half the dose each drug half-life because of its simplicity and maintenance of high serum levels; their two-patient cefazolin trial of this approach showed no significant accumulation.
The authors stated that a complete pharmacokinetic analysis of the data would be reported separately, so this article presents only a partial PK analysis.
The work was supported in part by the Veterans Administration and by a grant from Smith, Kline & French Laboratories.
